svg.title: trialSizing cheat sheet
svg.desc: One-page reference for the trialSizing R package: uniformity-trial basics, the five-step pipeline, accepted data shapes, checking the trial, CV by plot shape, fitting LRP/QRP/MCM plateau models, comparing methods, the Paranaiba closed form, number of replications, and exporting figures.
svg.text: Optimal plot size from a uniformity trial, and the replications needed to detect a given difference between treatment means.
A uniformity trial is a field sown uniformly —
one genotype, one management — and harvested
as a grid of small basic experimental units
plots lowers the CV, but the gain shrinks.
The optimal plot size Xo is where the CV
stops falling. CVxo, the CV expected there,
then sets the number of replications.
is the grid usable at all?
where does the CV level off?
Steps 1, 2 and 4 need the raw grid.
one trial; keeps the field layout
long data frame; grid rebuilt safely
Rows and columns are not interchangeable:
Three simulated 8 × 12 grids of 1 m² BEU,
free to redistribute. Pull one out with:
Before estimating anything, look at the grid: its
dimensions decide which shapes exist, and its
spatial structure is what the methods rest on.
#> rows cols n_shapes cv morans_i dependence
plot(chk) maps the field: a kriging surface
with the basic units on top, and fits a variogram.
Groups the BEU into every rectangular plot the
grid allows, one row per shape. Several shapes
share an area, so x repeats — give one CV
per shape, never the mean per size.
#> trial X_L X_C x n mean sd cv
X_L × X_C is the shape, x the area, n how
many plots it leaves. Large plots rest on few,
so n is the natural weight for a weighted fit.
Pass a trial column to fit one model per
trial. Works for every fitter, and for
Trials differ, as real trials do; the mean of the
All three take the CV table (or plain vectors)
and return Xo plus standardized statistics.

svg.text: Linear response plateau: a descending line
joined to a flat plateau. The breakpoint
comes from a grid search, so no starting
values are needed and the answer is the
joined smoothly to the plateau. The smooth
join always pushes the optimum out.
The optimum usually orders MCM < LRP < QRP.
The SSE profile of a broken line is stepped,
so several breakpoints can fit almost as
a few percent worse means Xo is not sharp.
Titles and styling belong to plot(), never
to the fitting call. plot() returns a ggplot,
Runs every applicable method on the same
data. Given a raw grid it builds the CV table
on the way, and Paranaiba joins in.
R2 and RMSE are recomputed on the original
CV scale, so they mean the same for every
method. AIC and BIC are left out on purpose.
With bootstrap = TRUE each Xo gets an
interval — often wider than the gap between
Works straight on the grid: estimates the
walk, then returns Xo in closed form — no
fitting, so no R2 or RMSE.
#> mean variance CV rho Xo CVxo
The walk follows the rows, as in the original
method. Both directions are always reported;
for CRD or RCBD. Feed it the CVxo of step 3.
